s0.why: [1] gives exactly this: coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock mostly of quartz, alkali feldspar, mica and plagioclase.

s1.why: [2] says high-silica, alkali-oxide-rich magma slowly cools and solidifies underground; [3] says it is common in continental crust.

s2.why: [8] says nearly always massive and tough; [9] says those properties made it a widespread construction stone throughout human history.

f0.why: [10] derives the word from Latin granum, a grain.

f1.why: [11] says granites can be predominantly white, pink or gray.

f2.why: [39] names rhyolite as the extrusive equivalent; volcanic is a fair gloss of extrusive.

f3.why: [35] gives average density between 2.65 and 2.75 g/cm3.

f4.why: [36] gives dry melting temperature at ambient pressure as 1215-1260 C.

q1.why: [39] states the extrusive equivalent of granite is rhyolite, which is the erupted, surface-cooled case.

q2.why: [8] says massive (lacking internal structures) and tough; [9] credits these for its use as construction stone.

q3.why: [36] says melting temperature is strongly reduced with water, down to 650 C at a few hundred MPa.

q4.why: [11] says the colour depends on mineralogy, so differing mineral mixes explain pink versus gray.

q5.why: [37] says poor primary permeability but strong secondary permeability through cracks and fractures.

q6.why: [10] says granum, a grain, refers to the coarse-grained structure of the rock.
